question: On 15 April, Thierry Breton, Commissioner for the Internal Market, called for the implementation of ‘truly effective [mirror] clauses’ applying ‘not only to products but also to production processes’, so that the same environmental standards are imposed on ‘European businesses and farmers’ and ‘their competitors’1.

However, the Commission’s proposals to Mercosur included an environmental addendum which did not involve ‘making the access of South American products to our market subject to compliance to the same environmental and health production standards as imposed on us’2. In February, the Veblen Institute highlighted Canada’s condemnation at the WTO of European environmental standards.

The Institute suggested that implementing mirror clauses and measures should go hand-in-hand with ‘reassessing the rules that govern international commerce, particularly in the WTO’, so ‘that Member States can make a legitimate distinction between products on the basis of the sustainability of their production processes’3.
As part of its ‘sustainability’ goals, is the Commission backing this ‘reassessment’ of WTO rules, and if so, how?

‘For a successful EU Competitiveness and Industry New Deal’ - LinkedIn - 17.4.2024. ‘Des filières interpellent Emmanuel Macron sur le Mercosur’ - La France Agricole - 1.12.2023. ‘Pourquoi est-il urgent de mettre en place des mesures miroirs? Un levier clé pour la transition agroécologique en Europe’ - Report by the Veblen Institute for Economic Reform - February 2024.
answer: In June 2022, the Commission adopted a report assessing in detail the opportunity and legal feasibility of applying EU health and environmental requirements to imported agri-food products (4). The report analyses the issue both in the case of free trade agreements and under autonomous EU legislation.

World Trade Organisation (WTO) rules provide a certain degree of flexibility in allowing its members to set requirements on imports. With respect to agri-food trade, current EU rules require all imports to comply with the EU’s health and safety product requirements. Non-compliant products cannot be placed on the EU market.

When it comes to requirements relating to process and production methods (PPM), the situation needs to be assessed case-bycase. Mirror provisions can be applied when necessary to address specific policy objectives, such as protection of public morals, protection of human, animal or plant health or global environmental concerns.

The application of PPM regulations to imported products in these fields must be done in full respect of WTO rules and other international commitments. Notably, these measures must be designed and applied in a non-discriminatory manner and not with a protectionist intent.

During this Commission mandate, the EU has issued several ambitious autonomous measures related to process and production methods (5), following a thorough case-by-case assessment, to ensure WTO compatibility.

The EU is also engaging in the WTO and other multilateral fora to promote internationally agreed sustainability standards, and use its network of bilateral free trade agreements as a platform for cooperation on sustainability issues with partners.
